source_text:
εὑρίσκομεν ἐν λογισμοῖς τὰ ἀποκαλυφθέντα ἡμῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ κηρύττομεν αὐτά, οὐ
λόγοις καλλωπίζοντες ἀλλὰ τὰ πνευματικὰ τοῖς πνευματικοῖς συγκρίνοντες,
πνεύματος δυνάμει τὰς ἐκείνου ἀποκαλύψεις καὶ νοοῦντες καὶ ἐν τάξει
κηρύττοντες. Πνευματικὰ πνευματικοῖς συγκρίνοντες· ὅταν γὰρ ἡ δευτέρα
ἀποκάλυψις ἑρμηνεία ᾖ τοῦ προτέρου καὶ σαφήνεια, συγκρίνοντες οἱ δεχόμενοι τὰς
ἀποκαλύψεις τὰ δεύτερα τοῖς πρώτοις, καὶ τὰ αὐτὰ εὑρίσκοντες πληροφορίαν
μείζονα ἐλάμβανον τῆς ἀποκαλυφθείσης ἀληθείας. 233,ξολ2.Ὁ μὲν θεὸς καὶ τὸ
πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον πρόσωπά ἐστιν δύο, ἄνθρωπος δὲ καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ οὐ δύο
πρόσωπα ἀλλ' εἶς ἄνθρωπος. ἀλλὰ τοῦτο λέγει· ὥσπερ ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ οὐκ ἔστι
διαφωνία γνώσεως, οὕτως καὶ ἐπὶ πατρὸς καὶ πνεύματος γνῶσις μία, ὥστε κατὰ
τοῦτο οὐκ ἂν ὡς ἀγνοοῦν ἠρεύνησεν τὸ πνεῦμα. εἶτα πάλιν ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
εἶπεν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος οὐκ εἶπεν τὸ ἐν τῷ θεῷ
ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ. διαφορὰ δὲ πολλὴ τοῦ τε ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τοῦ ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ· 234,ξολ2
τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐν αὐτῷ συμπληρωτικόν ἐστι τοῦ ὅλου ἀνθρώπου, τὸ δὲ ἐξ αὐτοῦ τὸ
αἴτιον δείκνυσιν.Ἀκριβῶς τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ εἶπεν ὡς ζῶσαν καὶ
ἐνυπόστατον οὐσίαν, τὸ δὲ ἀκάθαρτον τοῦ κόσμου ὡς συμπληρωτικὸν αὐτοῦ τῆς
οὐσίας· μέρος γὰρ τῆς κτίσεως αὐτοῦ ὁ διάβολος κατὰ τὸ γεγενῆσθαι. ὅμως οὐχ
εὑρίσκομεν λογισμοῖς τὰ ἀποκαλυφθέντα ἡμῖν καλλωπίσαι, ἀλλὰ πνευματικοῖς
πνευματικὰ συγκρίνομεν, ὅταν ἡ δευτέρα ἀποκάλυψις ἑρμηνεία καὶ σαφήνεια
γένηται τοῦ πρώτου διδάγματος ἢ ὁράματος ἢ θαύματος· τὰ γὰρ δεύτερα τοῖς
πρώτοις συγκρίνονται καὶ τὰ αὐτὰ εὑρίσκονται. πληροφορίαν μεγίστην λαμβάνομεν
τῆς ἀληθείας ἐκ τῆς συμφωνίας. καὶ τοῦτο δὲ δηλοῖ τὸ συγκρίνοντες ἐξ ἐναντίου, καὶ
τοῦτο διακρίνοντες καὶ χωρίζοντες· βέλτιον δὲ τὸ πρότερον. 1 Kor 2,14–15 Ψυχικὸς
δὲ ἄνθρωπος οὐ δέχεται τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος. ψυχικὸν λέγει τὸν στοιχοῦντα τοῖς
οἰκείοις λογισμοῖς. 235 Μωρία γὰρ αὐτῷ ἐστιν. τοσοῦτον τὸ βάθος τῆς πνευματικῆς
ἀποκαλύψεως ὡς τοῖς σοφοῖς τοῦ κόσμου τούτου μωρίαν φαίνεσθαι· οὕτως
ἀχώρητος αὐτοῖς ἡ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀποκάλυψις. Τοῦ γὰρ ἁγίου πνεύματος χάρις δύναμιν
ἐπιδεικνυμένη ἤλεγχε τὸν τεχνικόν, οὐ τεχνικῶς ἀλλ' ἰσχύϊ τῶν θαυμάτων. Οἱ
πνευματικοὶ οὐ λογισμοῖς τοὺς λογισμοὺς ἀνατρέπουσιν, ἀλλὰ τὸν παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ
δεχόμενοι νοῦν καὶ τὴν ἐκεῖθεν ἀποκάλυψιν διαλέγονται, ὥστε ὁ ἀντιτασσόμενος
οὐ λογισμοὺς ἐλέγχει, ἀλλ' ἐναντιοῦται τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ γνώσει. διὰ τοῦτό φησιν· τίς γὰρ
ἔγνω νοῦν κυρίου, ὃς συμβιβάσει αὐτόν; ἡμεῖς δὲ νοῦν Χριστοῦ ἔχομεν, τοῦτ' ἔστι
τὴν γνῶσιν. 234,ξολ2 Ψυχικὸν δὲ λέγει τὸν στοιχοῦντα τοῖς οἰκείοις λογισμοῖς ἢ τὸν
νοσοῦντα τοῖς τῆς ψυχῆς λογισμοῖς καὶ μὴ ἐρρωμένον περὶ τὴν 235,ξολ2 γνῶσιν τῆς
ἀληθείας, ὥσπερ καὶ σαρκικὸν λέγει τὸν νοσοῦντα περὶ τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας καὶ
ἡδονῶν δοῦλον. οὕτως οὖν ὁ ψυχικὸς οὐ δύναται δεκτικὸς εἶναι τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀλλ'
οὕτως κεκάκωται τὴν ψυχὴν ὡς μωρίαν ἡγεῖσθαι τὴν οἰκονομίαν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τὴν
χάριν. καὶ οὐ δυνάμενος γνῶναι ὅτι πνευματικῶς ἀνακρίνεται. ὁ ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος
τεχνικοὺς ἐπιζητῶν λογισμοὺς ἐπὶ τοῦ σταυροῦ ὡς μωρὸν καὶ ἀπείθανον ἀπωθεῖται
τὸ κήρυγμα, καὶ μὴ ἀποβλέπων πρὸς τὰς τοῦ πνεύματος θαυματουργίας οὐδὲ νοῆσαι
ἔτι δύναται, ὅτι πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἀντιτάττεται ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ πνεύματος δυνάμεως
καὶ θαυματουργίας ἀπελεγχόμενος· τὸ γὰρ ἀνακρίνεται δηλοῖ τὸ ἀκριβῶς καὶ
ἐξητασμένως ἀπελέγχεται. ὁ δὲ πνευματικός, ὁ τετυχηκὼς πνεύματος δι' ὧν
ἐπιδείκνυσι σημείων, ἀπελέγχει μὲν πάντα τὰ παρὰ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐλέγχοντα κακῶς,
αὐτὸς δὲ ὑπ' οὐδενὸς ἀπελέγχεται. εἶτα καὶ πιστούμενος τὸν λόγον τὰ ἐκ τῆς
παλαιᾶς παρατίθησι καί φησιν. 1 Kor 2,16 Συμβιβάσει· διορθώσει. ἡμεῖς νοῦν ἔχομεν
pass_a_gloss: (Continuing: not only, he says, do we not) find by reasonings the things revealed to us, but we also preach them, not beautifying (them) with words but comparing spiritual things with spiritual, by power of the Spirit both understanding his revelations and preaching (them) in order. 'Comparing spiritual things with spiritual': for when the second revelation is interpretation of the former and clarification, those receiving the revelations, comparing the second things with the first and finding the same things, received greater full assurance of the revealed truth. [Second column, page 233, parallel to the 2:10-13 notes:] God and the Holy Spirit are two persons, but man and the spirit in him not two persons but one man. But this he says: as in a man there is no disagreement of knowledge, so also in the case of Father and Spirit knowledge is one, so that in this respect the Spirit would not have searched as being ignorant. Then again, in the case of the man he said 'the spirit in him', but in the case of the Holy Spirit he did not say 'the (one) in God' but 'the (one) from God'. And great is the difference between 'in him' and 'from God'. [page 234, col. 2] For 'in him' is completing the whole man, but 'from him' shows the cause. Exactly he called the Holy Spirit 'from God' as a living and subsisting substance, but the unclean (spirit) 'of the world' as completing its substance; for the devil (is) part of its creation according to having come to be. However, we do not find (it right) to adorn by reasonings the things revealed to us, but we compare spiritual things with spiritual, when the second revelation becomes interpretation and clarification of the first teaching or vision or wonder; for the second things are compared with the first and are found the same. We receive greatest full assurance of the truth from the agreement. And 'comparing' also signifies the opposite, namely 'distinguishing' and 'separating'; but the former is better. [Label 1 Cor 2:14-15.] 'But the soul-man does not receive the things of the Spirit.' He calls soul-man the one walking in line with his own reasonings. [page 235] 'For it is folly to him.' So great the depth of the spiritual revelation that to the wise of this world it appears folly; so uncontainable for them is the revelation of God. For the grace of the Holy Spirit, displaying power, refuted the technical (man), not technically but by strength of the wonders. The spiritual (people) do not overturn reasonings with reasonings, but receiving the mind from God and the revelation from there they discourse, so that the one opposing does not refute reasonings but opposes the knowledge of God. Because of this he says: 'for who knew the mind of the Lord, who will instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ' (1 Cor 2:16), that is, the knowledge. [Second column, pages 234-235, parallel to the 2:14-15 note:] He calls soul-man the one walking in line with his own reasonings, or the one sick in the reasonings of the soul and not strong regarding the knowledge of the truth, as he also calls fleshly the one sick regarding fleshly desires and slave of pleasures. So then the soul-man cannot be receptive of the truth, but has been so harmed in the soul as to consider folly the dispensation of God and the grace. 'And not being able to know, because he is examined spiritually.' The soul-man, seeking technical reasonings about the cross, thrusts away the preaching as foolish and unpersuasive, and not looking toward the wonder-workings of the Spirit, can no longer even understand that he sets himself against the truth, being refuted by the power and wonder-working of the Spirit; for 'is examined' signifies 'is refuted exactly and with scrutiny'. But the spiritual (man), who has obtained the Spirit, through the signs he displays refutes all the things wrongly refuting among the others, but he himself is refuted by no one. Then also, confirming the argument, he sets beside (it) the things from the Old (Testament) and says: [Label 1 Cor 2:16.] 'Will instruct': will correct. 'We have the mind' (… continues in the next section).
pass_b_english: …discover by reasoning what has been revealed to us; we also proclaim it. We do not dress it up in fine words but "compare spiritual things with spiritual," grasping his revelations by the power of the Spirit and proclaiming them in due order. "Comparing spiritual things with spiritual": when a second revelation interprets and clarifies the earlier one, those who received the revelations compared the later with the earlier, found them the same, and so gained a firmer assurance of the truth revealed.

The second catena form adds: Of a man he said "the spirit that is in him," but of the Holy Spirit he did not say "that is in God"; he said "that is from God." There is a great difference between "in him" and "from God." He was exact when he called the Holy Spirit "from God," as a living being with its own subsistence, and the unclean spirit "of the world," as something that fills out the world's substance; for the devil is part of its creation, in that he came into being. The word "comparing" can also be taken in the opposite sense, as "distinguishing" and "separating"; but the first sense is better.

On 1 Corinthians 2:14–15: "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit." By "natural" he means the man who keeps in step with his own reasonings. "For they are folly to him." So deep is the spiritual revelation that to the wise of this world it looks like folly, so far beyond their grasp is God's revelation. The grace of the Holy Spirit, as it displayed its power, refuted the man of technique, and not by technique but by the force of its wonders. Spiritual people do not overturn reasonings with reasonings. They receive the mind that comes from God and the revelation that comes from there, and they speak from that, so that whoever opposes them is not refuting reasonings but setting himself against the knowledge of God. That is why he says, "For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ" (1 Corinthians 2:16), that is, his knowledge.

The second catena form adds: Or he means the man who is sick in the reasonings of his soul and is not sound in his grasp of the truth, just as he calls "fleshly" the man who is sick with fleshly desires and a slave of pleasures. So the natural man cannot take the truth in. His soul has been so damaged that he thinks God's dispensation and grace are folly. "And he cannot know, because he is examined spiritually." The natural man looks for clever arguments about the cross and pushes the preaching away as foolish and unconvincing. Because he does not look to the wonders the Spirit works, he can no longer even see that he is setting himself against the truth while the power and wonders of the Spirit refute him. "Is examined" means that he is refuted closely and after scrutiny. But the spiritual man, who has received the Spirit, uses the signs he displays to refute everything that others wrongly bring as refutation, while he himself is refuted by no one. Then, to confirm the argument, he cites the Old Testament as well and says:
On 1 Corinthians 2:16: "Will instruct" means "will correct." "We have the mind…

is examined, is refuted on scrutiny

choices.english: collapsed; new material printed after 'The second catena form adds:'
choices.why: Second-column forms of the 2:10-13 notes translated in u01-rem-close. Kept only what has no counterpart: the explicit 'in him' / 'from God' contrast, 'living being with its own subsistence', and the second sense of 'comparing'.
rejected: printing the whole second form (old English)

choices.english: printed after 'The second catena form adds:' minus its first clause
choices.why: Only the opening definition of ψυχικός repeats the first form; the rest has no counterpart and is translated in full.
The usual English for the lemma; the note itself explains it as the man led by his own reasonings and sick in his soul.
Severianus reads the verb of the man himself ('is refuted'), as his gloss shows; the English follows his reading, not the standard one.
Edition labels; the old English printed a bare '1 Cor 2:14-15' and '(1 Cor 2:16)'.
